portion_doctrine: Segments 1-10 of MOODBOARDING_DOC_OG are primarily transcribed video tutorials and Reddit discussions about mood boarding across multiple design disciplines (fashion photography, industrial design, logo design, product photography). Content is 85% boilerplate (transcription artifacts, navigation UI, promotional content, video timestamps). Real operative content: 5 repeatable mood board methodologies, specific tool stacks, and photography-specific direction tactics. No contradictions detected - all sources align on core purpose (visual alignment + team communication). High junk-to-gold ratio but gold is directly actionable for BJ's Direction Stack positioning.
operating_rules: Mood board purpose: create a visual box to contain ideas and prevent scope creep (prevents team from stepping outside the direction)
Structure mood boards into 5-10 sections: Title/Overview, Lighting, Hair+Makeup, Styling/Wardrobe, Poses/Shapes, Props, General Vibe, Background/Set
Send mood boards to team/model with 1-2 weeks advance notice minimum (allows preparation and gathering of materials)
Put physical printed copy on set + digital copy shared electronically to prevent idea theft and ensure team stays aligned during execution
Use mood boards in three phases: pre-production (client approval), on-set (team reference), post-production (editor alignment)
Include shoot title + date + client name on every mood board (clarity for distributed teams)
Credit all reference images; note photographer/source to prevent team from passing inspiration as original work
Separate design (polish/fonts/layout) from content (image selection); polish signals care but content/curation is primary value
Mood board effectiveness measured by: (1) client says yes, (2) team preparation improves, (3) shoot flow accelerates, (4) fewer reshoot/adjustments needed
For newer practitioners: 10 good images > 5 images; coherence matters more than volume; consistency of tone across images beats variety
Avoid formula/template fatigue: shift layout style between projects so mood boards don't feel repetitive across portfolio
Model/talent sections show movement + fluency needed, not just head shots; include full-body and portrait angles for team clarity
named_methods: 5-Page Mood Board Structure: Title, Lighting, Hair+Makeup, Styling, Poses+Shapes (scalable to 8-10 pages for high-budget work)
Photoshop Grid Method: Create 13-slot template using rulers/guides, paste images, free-transform to fit, use layer masks to crop spillover
Canva/Figma Approach: Drag-drop images into templates, adjust on-the-fly without grid constraints, easier for collaboration
Pinterest Collection Method: Create secret board, gather 13+ images matching theme, organize into folders (poses/makeup/styling/props), then translate into formal mood board
Mind Map First: Start with keywords (bold, striking, magical, playful), find images matching those words, build visual direction from conceptual anchor points
Tethered Raw Processing During Shoot: Process mood board reference in Capture One/Adobe as you shoot to visualize final color grading in real-time
Physical + Digital Dual Distribution: Print one copy for set, email PDF to team, design with headers/footers showing photographer credit + project name on every page
Pose Board vs Mood Board Split: Mood board = aesthetic/tone (color/texture/vibe), Pose Board = structural reference (desaturated, high-contrast, shapes only)
Template Recycling: Build reusable grid templates in Photoshop (5x box layout, 3x3 grid, Pinterest-style asymmetric) to speed production
Gobo + Multi-Light Visualization: Use mood board lighting section to show specific modifiers (Westcott Optical Spot, umbrella diffusion, colored gels) so team knows exact gear intent
numbers: 5 pages minimum for standard mood board (Title, Lighting, Hair+Makeup, Styling, Poses)
8-10 pages for high-budget commercial/advertising shoots with client approval cycle
13 images typical grid size (fits A4 print cleanly, 4-5 per section)
10 good photos > 5 photos (quality + consistency over minimalism)
5 lighting reference images recommended (shows lighting consistency, not single example)
2 weeks advance notice to model/team (allows wardrobe/prep gathering)
1-2 weeks before shoot publish mood board to team (not day-of)
1-5% border on A4 doc standard (5% = proportionate whitespace, visual breathing room)
3 strobes typical for complex lighting setup (main + background + fill), communicated in mood board
24-48 hours for team to review + respond to mood board before commitment deadline
tools: Adobe Photoshop (layer-based grid method, smart objects, color overlays, free-transform masking)
Figma / FigJam (collaborative, segment-able sections, shared real-time, infinite canvas)
Pinterest (image discovery, secret boards, easy sharing via link)
Google Docs (lightweight, collaborative, quick image embedding)
Capture One (tethered RAW processing during shoot for real-time color grading visualization)
Adobe Illustrator (typography/layout control, for print-ready mood boards)
Mood.site (free app, no signup, auto-layouts mood boards)
HP Advanced Photo Paper (physical print medium, professional feel)
prompts: Client Personality Slider: Ask client on 1-10 scale: Elite vs Mass Appeal, Serious vs Playful, Minimal vs Maximal, Traditional vs Futuristic. Map competitors on same slider to show where brand sits.

Mind Map Anchor: Start mood board by writing 4-6 keywords (bold, striking, magical, playful, professional). Find images matching each keyword. Build visual frequency alignment before selecting final images.

Direction Conversation with Team: Show reference image, ask makeup artist: 'What do you see about her face that you'd emphasize?' Ask stylist: 'Given this wardrobe direction, what fabrics/textures feel right?' Pre-emptively ask for their ideas vs directive dictation.

Lighting Specificity Question: Instead of 'bright lighting', ask 'Are you shooting hard light (crisp shadows, dramatic) or soft light (diffused, flattering)?' Show 5 reference images of the chosen approach.
Pose Energy Frame: 'Is the energy relaxed/calm, playful/energetic, or strong/powerful?' Show pose references matching that energy tier. Don't mix energy levels across pose board.
Before Design, Ask: 'What doesn't belong in this mood board?' (removes ambiguous items faster than asking what does belong)
Feedback Loop: After sharing mood board, ask 'Does this feel like us to you? What's missing? What feels off?' vs assuming silence = approval.
skills: Visual tone recognition: identifying consistent mood across disparate images
Reference photo curation: finding 10 good images in 30 min vs 2 hours of scrolling
Grid + composition: spacing, alignment, white space hierarchy on mood board itself
Team communication through visual constraint: using mood board to prevent scope creep + scope conversations mid-shoot
Lighting communication to non-technical team: translating hard/soft/color into visual reference vs jargon
Collaborative feedback loops: asking questions vs stating direction, getting team buy-in before shoot day
Aesthetic consistency: matching color tone, texture weight, subject matter across images so mood board doesn't feel scattered
Client ego play: understanding mood board title + polish sells confidence ('This photographer has already won'), not just images
Template design: building reusable Photoshop/Figma templates that speed production without feeling formulaic
gates: Mood board must be finalized + distributed 1-2 weeks before shoot (not 3 days before)
Every image on mood board must have source attribution (photographer credit line or URL)
Mood board must include shoot title, date, client name, photographer name on title + every page footer
Lighting section must show 5+ reference images of the chosen lighting approach (not single example)
Pose section must reference movement/fluency, not just static positioning
Team must receive mood board via PDF email + physical print by photographer (prevents 'lost' excuse)
Before client approval, mood board must be reviewed by creative team for alignment (makeup/stylist/model weigh in)
Mood board grid must be clean (no overlap, no bleeding across boxes, OR intentional asymmetric style carried through consistently)
content_ideas: Tutorial: How to build a Photoshop mood board grid template for reuse (save 30 min per project)
Checklist: 10-point mood board review before sharing with client (covers lighting, wardrobe, poses, credit, date, title)
Video: Direction Stack application to mood boards (showing how poses/expression/energy direction translates to mood board language)
Comparison post: Mood boards that sold the client vs mood boards that confused the client (what works vs what fails)
Client communication template: Email script for requesting mood board feedback from non-designer clients
Advanced: Using Capture One tethered processing during shoot to refine mood board color grading in real-time
Case study: How mood boards reduce reshoot requests + revisions (data on time saved)
Brand positioning angle: Mood boards as proof-of-concept for premium photographers (cheap photographers skip them, premium ones invest the time)
weird_gold: Mood board title page as ego play: Make it beautiful enough that client's confidence is inflated BEFORE seeing the actual shoot plan. Emotional decision-making > logical. (Contrasts with typical 'mood board is just reference')

Pose Board desaturation hack: Remove color from pose reference board so team focuses on SHAPES/STRUCTURE not aesthetics. Prevents pose misinterpretation due to color appeal. (Tactical constraint that improves execution)

Gobo projection for lighting mood: You can project patterns onto background to mimic mood (Valentino runway inspiration). Visualized in mood board lighting section = team understands intent without on-set confusion.

Reddit designer counter-argument: '20-year professional never used a mood board.' vs 'mood boards are the only thing that stopped freelance chaos.' Both true. Mood boards are force-multiplier for teams; unnecessary for solo operators.

Template fatigue rule: If you use same 13-box grid for every project, portfolio LOOKS formulaic to clients. Vary grid layout (5-box, 3x3, asymmetric) between projects even if client doesn't see it. Signals intentionality.

Physical printout ritual: Digital mood boards get lost in team Slack/email. Physical print on set + copies at every station (hair, makeup, stylist) = 3x less 'did you get the brief' friction during shoot.

Mind mapping before images: Most tutorials start with image collection. The operating insight: start with 4-6 keywords, THEN find images. Keyword-first = visual frequency alignment. Images-first = scattered aesthetic.

Hard light washing out makeup = heavy makeup needed: For fashion/editorial with hard light, makeup must be 2x heavier than normal to read on camera. Mood board makeup section signals this to makeup artist without directive.'
